Briefly explain why each of the following are not valid non-functional requirements. (i) The kitchen staff must finish the customer order within 10 minutes of receiving it. (ii) The system must count up all menu items ordered, and display the statistics on request.

recall.a: Governs staff, not software (business rule); counts-and-displays is a function (FR in disguise). Both fail in-scope/non-functional properties.
recall.q: Why do the two 2019 Q3(c) requirements fail?

sections.heading: How NFR marks are lost
bullets: Calling a function an NFR (2022 Q3.2a, 2019 Q3c-ii counting statistics).
Calling a business rule an NFR (2019 Q3c-i kitchen timing governs staff).
Leaving 'user friendly' unquantified instead of rewriting with user/task/bound/criterion.
Proposing a reliability metric that mismatches usage (POFOD for continuous monitoring).
Writing 'perfect reliability' or unbounded performance ('as fast as possible').
Omitting the environment from performance bounds.

summary: Six NFR mark-losers: disguised functions, business rules, unquantified adjectives, mismatched metrics, perfection claims, missing environments.
title: NFRs: common exam mistakes

activities.prompt: POFOD is the right metric for a continuously displayed vital-signs monitor.

distractor.0: Continuous display has no discrete 'demands' — availability (uptime fraction) fits. POFOD suits on-demand checks like ticket validation.

activities.explanation: False — the classic metric mismatch. Match the metric to the usage pattern or the requirement is nonsense.
